imageIntegrations.caption: Before growth-plate closure, excess hGH can produce excessive long-bone lengthening and height (gigantism). After closure, excess hGH does not increase long-bone length or height; bones and soft tissues can enlarge (acromegaly). Simplified comparison, not to scale.
imageIntegrations.alt: Matched cutaway long-bone ends show an open cartilage growth plate on the left and a fused plate on the right. Excess hGH before closure can increase long-bone length and height; after closure it does not increase long-bone length or height, although bones and soft tissues can enlarge.

imageIntegrations.caption: ADH is produced in the hypothalamus and released into the blood by the posterior pituitary. In normally responsive kidneys, more ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability. More water moves by osmosis from forming urine, through the duct wall and surrounding tissue, back toward blood. Urine volume decreases and urine becomes more concentrated. Lower ADH produces the opposite relative pattern. Arrows represent relative net water movement, not measured rates or molecular pumps. Tissue spacing is simplified and not to scale.
imageIntegrations.alt: Two collecting-duct cutaways compare lower and higher ADH. Each separates yellow forming urine, the epithelial duct wall, surrounding tissue and red blood vessel. A small blue arrow on the lower-ADH side and three larger arrows on the higher-ADH side run from lumen through the wall toward blood. Higher ADH gives smaller-volume, more concentrated urine when kidneys respond normally.

imageIntegrations.caption: The hypothalamus releases TRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH. TSH stimulates thyroid-hormone secretion. Thyroxine (T4) is used here to represent thyroid hormone; thyroid hormones affect metabolism, growth and development and reduce upstream TRH and TSH stimulation in a normally functioning control pathway. Feedback reduces TRH and TSH release; it does not permanently switch these glands off. T3 and conversion of T4 to T3 are omitted simplifications. Green arrows show forward stimulation. Red T-bars show inhibition by thyroid-hormone feedback. This is a simplified functional pathway, not complete organ anatomy, a measured concentration chart or an account of every molecular step; it is not to scale.
imageIntegrations.alt: A vertical sequence connects hypothalamus, anterior pituitary, thyroid gland and body tissues with green arrows labelled TRH, TSH and Thyroxine (T4). A red route branches from the thyroid-hormone signal and ends in inhibitory T-bars at both hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.

imageIntegrations.caption: Falling blood calcium stimulates PTH release from the parathyroid glands. PTH promotes calcium mobilization from bone and increases kidney calcium reabsorption. PTH also promotes kidney activation of vitamin D to calcitriol, which increases intestinal calcium absorption; the intestinal effect shown is indirect. As blood calcium rises toward its usual range, the stimulus for extra PTH decreases. Blue symbols represent calcium ions and arrows represent net movement into blood, not complete molecular transport mechanisms. This illustration isolates calcium movement: phosphate regulation and detailed bone-cell signalling are omitted. PTH does not simply retain every mineral. Calcitonin has a relatively minor role in adult-human calcium regulation and is not shown as a mirror-image controller. The renal panel uses generic renal epithelium, not segment-specific histology. Tissue sizes, spacing and ions are schematic, not to scale.
imageIntegrations.alt: Three tissue cutaways show calcium moving from bone mineral into blood, from kidney-tubule fluid through the wall back into blood, and from intestinal contents through gut epithelium into blood. The intestinal route names active vitamin D as the mediator of increased absorption.

imageIntegrations.caption: After a meal, pancreatic beta cells release insulin, promoting glucose use and storage, including glycogen formation in liver cells. Between meals, pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon, promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose release into blood. Glycogen stays inside cells; the released glucose can enter blood. This is only one part of blood-glucose regulation. Insulin also acts on other responsive tissues, including muscle and fat, and glucagon also supports new glucose production by the liver. Muscle glycogen mainly supports the muscle's own fuel needs. Both regulatory responses oppose their initiating glucose disturbance. Hexagons and branching are schematic symbols, not complete chemical structures or a step-by-step biochemical pathway; omitted metabolic intermediates are not shown. Not to scale.
imageIntegrations.alt: Two liver-cell cutaways beside blood vessels show opposite net routes. After a meal, blood glucose enters the liver-cell glucose pool and is stored as a branched glycogen polymer. Between meals, glycogen breakdown supplies glucose that leaves the liver cell and enters blood. Glycogen remains intracellular on both sides.
